review_text:
Poulet Rouge, Porcini Mushrooms, Kohlrabi Broth, Broccoli Rabe:  With both my slices of bread gone in no time flat it was time for a dish we'd been watching roast in the oven for at least the last forty five minutes and with juices streaming down the lean bird what we received would prove every bit worth the wait as crisp and salty skin gave way to juicy meat resting in a slightly bitter and aromatic broth of kohlrabi, mushrooms, and rabe.  With a portion of dark and white meat provided and the flavors both intense and clean my guess is that this bird was not aged like the rest of the meats but having never tasted this particular heritage breed I really cannot be sure.

Strawberry Buttermilk Gelato:  Arriving as a palate cleanser before our last savory of the evening this small quenelle of gelato was creamy and smooth with small bits of berry throughout, a nice flavor serving its purpose admirably.

85 Day Dry Aged Wagyu Beef, Hearts of Palm, Ramps, Scapes, Vin Cotto:  The other piece of meat sitting next to the lamb rack earlier in the night, this was by far my most anticipated course of the night and much like last time the ultra-aged meat did not disappoint.  A sizable portion, though certainly not the nearly half pound served during my previous visit, and prepared to medium rare with another piece pan seared to well-done at its side the only way to describe the flavor is "rich" with a touch of earthy funk nicely balanced by a touch of acid and the pungency of the tender ramps and scapes.

Bayley Hazen Blue Cheese with Fig, Radish, Walnuts, Fennel, Honeycomb from the Roof:  As if the Wagyu wasn't funky enough our cheese course for the evening would feature one of my favorite American Blues alongside a number of accoutrements and although the figs were slightly less sweet than I would have liked the pairing of Jasper Hill's finest cheese with both the aromatic fennel and the bitter radish was an inspired choice while the honeycomb and walnuts worked as well as expected in highlighting the subtle spicy notes of the cheese.

Chamomile Gelato with Quinoa and Chickpea Crumble:  Having been only modestly impressed with the desserts on Roberta's tasting the first time around I was happy to see the first of three options arrive with a lot more nuance than any during my first visit and with the gelato flavored similarly to the milky tea that my grandmother often served both me as a child I was additionally impressed by the "crumble" - a buttery composition tasting something like grapenuts cereal without the bitterness. 

Wild Strawberries, Strawberry Soup, Sorrel and Ground Ivy Granita, Lemon Verbena Ice Cream:  Following close on the heels of the gelato this inspired composition would not have been out of place on the menu at a place like Manresa or even L'Arpege and with myriad textures, temperatures, and flavors at play the overall effect was at times sweet and other times sour but at all times intensely herbal.  To quote one of my co-diners, it tasted "healthy" and "refreshing," a perfect dish for summer.

Cherry Sorbet, Yogurt, Coffee and Hempseed Crumble, Poached Cherries, Pakistani Noble Berry:  The final plate of the evening and the largest of the desserts suffice it to say that this was outstanding - the sorbet soft and creamy, the poached cherries slightly boozy, the yogurt just a touch sour, and the crumble much like the quinoa/chickpea combination in texture but laced with notes of coffee and earthiness in flavor.  Unfamiliar with the "Noble Berry" prior to this I was additionally impressed by the pastry chef taking time to chat with us about the ingredient, a jet black finger-length berry with a flavor similar to blackberries but a texture somewhat akin to a date.

Matcha:  Served after the desserts as we sat listening to music while watching the kitchen scrub down I personally would have preferred coffee, but all things being equal I'll never complain about green tea either, particularly one this fragrant.

The Verdict:  With the capability to now serve 12 persons per night when Carlo is in town I can only assume that Blanca will help the crew at Roberta's progress through their extensive wait list in a more expedited manner yet given the quality of the room, the food, the service, and the man in the kitchen I could also see the opposite occurring where demand increases even further and as such I will say the same thing I said after my last meal - that this is a dining experience that should reside near the top of everyone's 'must-visit' list, and that I cannot wait to go back.

The End.

last night we went to roberta's (which is now known as Blanca) for a 27 course tasting menu paired with 3 different wines (we should have just done the full wine pairing but i was worried about getting to drunk to go to work the next day - it didn't matter, i got drunk anyway). on the drive home we tried to recount each bite or dish with fuzzy, giddy, food coma-y heads. we did a decent job of recalling 25 of the 27 dishes and in no particular order and without the accouterments (some things had chrysanthemum leaves and cherries and rhubarb, ramps, garlic leaves and sprigs of this and that along with green/yellow and pink sauces) we came up with the below list:

Sturgeon Osetra Caviar with Goats Milk
Glass shrimp with Poppy Seeds
Jack Fish
Veal Sweet Bread
Uni & House Made Tofu
Soft Shell Crab with Yogurt Sauce
Squid with Meyer Lemon and Ramps 
Roasted Sweet Potato
Horse Mackerel
Perch (Slightly Seared)
Smoked Fish (such a meaty flavor)
Geoduck with cherry
Japanese clam
Rhubarb Gelato
Spot prawn
Carpaccio with Duck Egg
Lamb Pasta
Clam Pasta
Andouille Ravioli (heaven!)
85 Day Dry Aged Ribeye
Rack of Lamb & Mint Jelly with Coriander (crackely skin)
Heritage Bird (from Pennsylvania)
85 Day 
Cheese & Honey Comb
Quinoa Crumble
Coffee Crumble
Strawberry Shortcake (Roberta's version - my least favorite of all the dishes)

the dishes were divine. truly special. If you want to read food bloggers break it down in their sciency way that they do, i implore you to check out chowhound or pocketfork's review of roberta's tasting menu. 

the new tasting room seats 12 and opened in April. in the past, the tasting menu was happening twice a week and only seated 4. the new tasting room just allowed a lot of people wanting this reservation to finally have a shot. we waited 9 months before getting this call. 

it's an expensive meal. the tasting menu is $180 a person. wine pairing is an additional $85 or you can get several of their wines by the glass or half bottle. 

the food was amazing but there were definitely some kinks to work out with the wait staff.

Signed up for Roberta's tasting menu back in October '11 and finally got a callback for a May reservation.  We had no clue that there was a separate tasting room and were shocked to be led to the spotless new space a half block down from the regular entrance. So suffice it to say the hype train was full steam ahead by the time we sat down.

Say what you will about the new space...on the one hand, it feels a bit clinical compared to the charming, DIY rusticity of Roberta's. But I think the idea is that it's really about the food and nothing else. Little touches like the turntable, massive fish head, and super comfortable chairs make it less alienating. Also you have to check out the toilet, it's one of those indecipherable, 50-function Japanese things that I'm too scared to experiment with. 

There's no question $180 is a stiff entry fee. But on the plus side, you won't be getting B-grade talent prepping your cuisine. They only do tastings if head chef and creative genius Carlo Mirarchi is there. Watching him break down proteins and plate the intricate dishes was something to see. I for one would rather pay the $180 and watch this kitchen at work than suffer through some overblown Broadway production.    

The food is as you'd expect: immensely creative, high technique, and hyperexotic ingredients you won't be spotting on freshdirect anytime this century.  Some courses were more unforgettable than others (the funk-laden dry-aged ribeye, in particular, is like nothing I've had before). The service was impeccable for how new this tasting space was...organized, friendly, passionate about the food, and, perhaps most importantly, bringing a fun attitude that ensured everyone had a great time.

Why not 5 stars? I felt the wine pairing could be improved. We were told that they were still in the development phase building the cellar, so perhaps it's gotten better in the weeks since. But notwithstanding that, I'll be stunned if Blanca doesn't have a fistful of Michelin stars in its future.

Ok folks.   I went here a while ago and I just couldn't get my act together to write about the exquisiteness of Blanca.  But after reading the review by a fellow yelper wanting to give Blanca zero stars, I felt it was time to set the record straight.  Blanca is a super special experience.  I love what Carlo is doing and kudos to him for taking the risk, trying to make a unique experience in a sketchy place like bushwick!

My friend read about Robertas in the new York times review.  He dutifully put himself on the waiting and after 7 months (egads!), he finally got a ressie.  I was the lucky date and on opening night to boot!  

To be honest, this is going back two months.  The meal,the chefs table and the vibe were awesome.  They had a turntable with records a la Barry manilow, Neil diamond etc.  and we had cutest waitress who looked like a young Mia farrow.  It's all tasting menu and 20 or so little courses which we opted to do the wine pairing.  I think the wine / beer ale pairing needs a bit of work (limited) but that's the only black mark I can give this place.  

So if you want a detail of the food.  Refer to Michael u's review.  Blanca is a beautiful, tasting room lab where Carlo is creating.  Close your eyes and pay the price.  (I didn't pay but I venture to guess $300 +with tax and tip)    It's a unique experience that you won't forget.

Had the pleasure of having dinner at Blanca last night. Made my e-mail request for a reservation way back in February which was answered with thanks for your interest but we are completely booked up until the end of April. We will put you on the wait list in the order your request was received. I had forgotten about my request until late June when I sent off an e-mail to see where I stood on the wait list. I was pleasantly surprised to receive an e-mail reply a day later that a cancellation had opended up a few spots for dinner on Saturday July 08th. So needless to say I jumped at the chance and snapped up 2 spots in order to see if all the hype is justified or is it some hipster mirage deep in the Bush. Well I am happy to give a resounding YES!!! Blanca lived up to and far exceeded the hype. Which is rare these days in the foodie frenzied internet blogging world. I will refrain from discussing the menu since others have already done that at length on this site. Yes, the area may be sketchy to some but the trek out is worth it. Chef Carlo executed the evening with precision and was engaging at the end of service which is all you can ask for. I have been fortunate enough to dine at many of the so called best restaurants in NYC & beyond. This meal rated highly amongst them. The Chef & staff can be proud and will only fine tune this culinary machine in the future. I would like to wish Chef Carlo Mirachi luck but he doesn't need it. He has something far better. Skill & determination. 

Also a shout out to the somellier who did a wonderful job with the wine pairing incorporating sake & beer into the evening. Job well done with some daring choices. BRAVO!!!!!

I'd been on the Roberta's Tasting menu waitlist so long, Chef Mirarchi opened Blanca's. I recently got an email saying they were ready for me when I had put myself on the list 5 months ago. I'd long left NYC by this email but luckily for me Chef Mirarchi brought the Blanca tasting menu to me. Being good friends with Chef David Kinch we were in for a special treat of Blanca-Manresa tag team. I may miss out on the divey Roberta's or the new fangled Blanca's 12 seat spaces, but it's the food that you're going for right?

We sat down to a fantastic 4.5 hours of glorious dishes as follows:

-turnip, porchini, goat's milk, caviar, kumquat

-Nude and raw, Veal and albacore, olive and truffle "battuta"
2002 Laurent Perrier Millesime

-Bonito, lightly smoked, succulents (sea bean, white borage, purslane)
2004  Trimbach Cuvee Frederic Emile Riesling Alsace

-Shellfish and sorrels, narsturtium and saffron
2007 Tyrell's Wines Semillon Reserve Hunter Valley Australia

-Raviolo, anise hyssop and pecorino, N'duja
2010 Domaine Ott Chateau de Sell Rose Cote de Provence France

-Abats d'agneau, beets roasted with blueberry, fiorelli
2004 August Kessler Spatburgunder (Pinot Noir) Rheingau Germany

-80 Day Dry Aged Beef Loin, necatarine, sauce of aged far and vin cotto, aliums
2006 Paolo Bea Rosso de Veo Sagrantino Umbria Italy

-Buckwheat shortbread, plum, elderflower-lychee sorbet
-Apricot cremeaux, puffed and fried rice, apricot pit sherbert
2006 Chateau Les Justices Sauternes

Now I'd heard many things about Chef Mirarchi's cooking and after long, long last I finally got  to try it. The bonus was it was basically in my own back yard. Things like the 80 day dry aged beef was super intense. It was almost too much of a good thing. Some of the dishes put out were totally outside of what I thought we'd get, especially the influences of many cultures.

After the dinner was finished Carlo came out with his Red, White and Blue American Flag Budweiser, with a great laugh and totally down to earth for such talent. We'd run into him a couple more times in the next few days at a party and a dinner. A great guy and I can't say enough about the food. True skill and I look forward to the meals when Im in town in his hood.

After only being "open to the public" for a few weeks now (they were working through a monster waiting list for a while before taking new reservations), I couldn't help but hit up another extreme 3 hour plus tastefest in Brooklyn after having such a good time at Chef's Table at Brooklyn Fare about a year ago.

The service was top notch.  Our waiters and waitresses were more than friendly, happy to discuss the food, the story behind the space, and answer our random questions all throughout the night.  Granted, one would expect that with several staff members and only 12 guests per evening.  On that note, the space was very comfortable compared to Brooklyn Fare.  There was a nice amount of space between you at the kitchen, an airy high ceiling, and you didn't have to squeeze around the edges to make it to the bathroom.  The highlight of the ambiance had to be the record player where you can put out albums to have them play throughout the night.  Nothing like stringing together Hall & Oates, A-ha, Simon & Garfunkel, and then Metallica. 

The food was tasty (this is a five star review after all), through there were few moments that left me completely shocked like I have been during other tasting menus (such as the sometime intense but totally appropriate flavors at Brooklyn Fare, the wow factor of some courses at Eleven Madison Park, the theme approach of Torrisi, etc.).  That is not to say that anything tasted bad and I didn't lick the plate clean, simply nothing left a lasting, wake-up-in-a-cold-sweat-after-a-flashback sort of impression.  If you like fresh food cooked well, where you can actually taste the underlying ingredient and appreciate its origin, then this is the place for you.  

One last note--the wine pairing was particularly good, so I would definitely recommend the splurge.  Put your food in the hands of the chef, the wine in the hands of your server, and simply focus on if you should play The Rolling Stones or Fleetwood Mac for the next record...



...who am I kidding. The answer is clearly The Rolling Stones.

ambitious add to Roberta's real estate. and the label dinner theater is apt: a parade of one-bite wonders (27) prepared at showcase kitchen across from a dozen plush counter seats. not a very original concept, seen recently at Agapè Substance in Paris, El Bulli many years before. the farms, seas, the butcher; and foams, powder, gelée all present, with a decidedly Bushwick spin. at $180+ prix fixe, bit dear, uneven and tiresome. i prefer down-home Roberta's. http://www.yelp.com/user_details_review_search?userid=-Uch0Ftb3uw09Vkm1PBeog&q=roberta%27s
Amazing food. Service super. Wine pairing one of the best deals in town. Its worth waiting to get a reservation. Its a true labor of love.  Who knew this spectacular treat was hiding in the garden?

This place is awesome.  Loved the room it was in: bright, light and airy.  Lotsa space between diners on the counter surrounding the open kitchen.  Very different from Roberta's itself.  Tasting menu style, lasted about 3-3.5 hours.  In general, food was incredible.  A few stand-out dishes, a few very good dishes, and only a couple that were less memorable.  My personal favorite: dry aged beef.  For 85 days!!!  So crazy.  Worth it just for that.  Not stuffy at all. I liked it better than Brooklyn Fare because no chef is like watching your every move and you can take pics and do whatever.  I did, however, like Atera better (another tasting menu format place I went to recently) just because the food techniques and presentation were a bit more unique.  

More details of my visit posted on my blog!  http://photo-hungry.com/post/31068215047/blanca  

Couldn't post all the pics tho cos they requested us not to, so only posted those already posted by Time Out, NYTimes or Bon Appetit (altho I see most of them are posted on yelp already too).  Definitely a must go foodie destination - start trying to make rez now tho!

Forget about the fact that you have to trek to Bushwick, or the difficult reservation policy, or the required 6 p.m. start time.  Forget all about those things.  You may find any or all of things somewhat inconvenient or slightly annoying, but the payoff will be, bar none, one of the best meals of your life and an experience of a lifetime.  

We had dinner there last night, a Friday evening.  To enter Blanca, you must first enter Roberta's.  You are greeted warmly and politely asked to wait at the bar inside Roberta's or outside in the back garden courtyard until the 6 p.m. seating commences.  At the anointed hour, the host comes to each individual party, chats with you on a first name basis, and separately guides each party through the back courtyard into Blanca.  What an amazing touch.

The space - essentially a 12 seat bar surrounding an open kitchen - as seen in various reviews, is sparkling clean, modern, and pleasantly lighted.  The bar seats are luxurious leather with a high back - a much needed respite from the uncomfortable wooden stools at some of the city's others similar establishments, and perfect for almost 4 hours of time that you will be spending inside.

The menu consisted of 29 courses.  Yes, 29 courses!  Some were only a bite, some a few bites, and some a few more than that.  The courses ranged from shellfish preparations, various beef creations, lamb, intricate pastas, crudo/sashimi items, amazing Roberta's bread, dessert courses, and the like  According to the amazingly friendly staff, these courses are ever-changing.  To describe each one in detail would (a) be impossible to recall due to the sheer number and (b) would be a disservice to those of you who have not yet been here.  Instead, come here with an open mind, a refined palate, an empty stomach and prepare to be absolutely wowed.  Do yourself a favor and do not stop to take a picture of every course that comes through - stay in the moment and enjoy the experience.

We, along with all 12 others, got the wine pairings as well at $85/pp.  Well worth it.  The pairings including whites, reds, sake, beers, champagne and ciders, and were poured generously.  Highly recommend this, and prevents drinking too much to enjoy the food, as a lot of bottles of wine could conceivably be consumed over a four hour meal.

In the front corner of the restaurant, there is a 1970s-looking turntable, lots of great records and a vintage stereo.  Diners are encouraged to take a look as the night goes on and play some of their favorite tracks.  I did so, and so did most of the others, most of whom became quick friends over the course of this incredible evening.  Want to stop for a minute and pop "Purple Rain" on to the turntable?  Go for it!  It is another amazing touch and adds to the friendly, fun, and unpretentious atmosphere Chef Carlo and his team have created - which in my view is one of the primary things that separates Blanca from its competitors.  Those "other" places are also unpretentious, but not nearly as friendly, fun and comfortable.  At Blanca, there is a communal beauty to the experience - but at the same time, you are not robbed of the intimacy you may be seeking when spending this amount of money on a meal.  It is a rare combination, when combined with quality of the food, creates a perfect storm of unsurpassed excellence that I have never felt at a restaurant.

Even after the almost 4 hour gastronomic extravaganza, many of us were relaxing and chatting with Chef Carlo and his staff for 20-30 minutes, playing records and reveling in the awesomeness.  When we finally departed, Chef Carlo personally walked us out of the restaurant, through the garden and all the way to the sidewalk, and thanked us for about the 15th time.  I cannot imagine another Chef of his magnitude doing such a thing.

Absolutely delicious, and a fantastic experience.  2nd best meal I've had in New York!

Practically every dish was superb.   (there were 2 exceptions, but even still those 2 dishes weren't bad).

The service is spot on.

The decor is simple and clean.

We had 2 bottles of wine.  They were okay, but didn't impress me.

Still, all in all an excellent experience with delicious food and excellent service.  I would extremely happily go again!

This meal lacked the consistency I had hoped for, but a night at Blanca is a uniquely jovial experience. 

The service was outstanding, and the atmosphere was perfectly comfortable (and gleefully boozy). The entire staff was gregarious and knowledgable. It was nice to wander over to the record table to put on music. This meal was a lot of fun. 

The food was alternately remarkable and simply tasty. A handful of the 20+ dishes were absolutely delicious, and I wouldn't have changed a thing. Unfortunately, several dishes were near-misses; some needed another flavor, and some compositions didn't lend themselves to the small-plate format (almost every dish is 1-4 bites). I think expanding some dishes out into full plates (and perhaps cutting down on the total course number) would better suit Chef Mirarchi's skills. 
 
I generally don't like to make comparisons between restaurants, but it's helpful, I think, to compare this meal to its closest analogue in NYC -- Chef's Table at Brooklyn Fare. While Chef's Table lacked Blanca's joviality and warmth, its cuisine was absolutely stunning from start to finish. Each dish was a marvel of flavor and composition. I wish I could say the same about Blanca's food. Blanca has many charms and Chef Mirarchi does some great things -- the food was just not as remarkable as I wanted it to be.

By far the best chefs table I've been at.

Many in the past were sorely disappointing but this really brought it.

Intimate, fun, informative, secretive, and relaxing on a variety of levels.  

They nailed over 25 of the nearly 30 courses at least, and the others were still better than anything I've had in recent months.

You will not be disappointed.

Excellent!! Great ingredients and perfectly executed. What really took it all home was the service. I have to say the staff is super nice, welcoming and  does everything to make it an unforgettable experience. Will be back in a few months if I can get a reservation.

I don't think the question is what did I like about Blanca.... but rather .... what do I love more? Is it the warm cozy feeling when I walk into the restaurant after battling the Nor'easter? Is it the friendly staff and chefs that just chat with you during the whole meal? Or is it the 28 course meal that leaves me nostalgic the next day? I just can't decide.

What I do know is that everything make the experience fabulous and worthwhile. My boyfriend and I came here for our 2 year anniversary and we were not disappointed. 

To enter Blanca, you have to go through Roberta's... through their garden . The restaurant itself, is simple and inviting with 12 seats around the bar. 

There is around 28 courses and served over a span of 3 hours or so. My favorites were: beef carpaccio with duck egg yolk, scallops, cooked oyster, all the meat dishes, and a dessert dish with celery soup and sorbet. It is hard to recollect all the ingredients as we were just trying to enjoy our dishes.

Right now it may be the hottest and best chef's table in America.

This is the back part of the hot and always crammed Roberta's.

Great atmosphere and a dizzying array of small delicious morsels. Great service and pairings to provide you a chance to experience dining in a more casual way.

Part of the new hipster revival of Brooklyn, elevating it to the same heights as Manhattan, you really can't go wrong here.

12 seats, vinyl to spin as you like, Chef Mirarchi is doing something truly inspiring here.

Now I'm not going to repeat what has already been written by other intelligent reviews posted for this restaurant, because for the most part, they are right on (I wonder if there is a correlation between people who appreciate great food experiences and intelligence? :-) )
I'm not new to the world of multi-course dinner experiences. And I'm not going to say that this was the best food experience that I have ever had because I don't like ranking something so subjective. It's like saying you have a favorite child, when in fact you'd take bullet for any one of them.
What I really liked is how they used excellent, sourced ingredients as their focus in creating a menu. Much like a celebration of freshness and availability taken to the edge! They didn't have to rely on just the use of expensive ingredients to justify their specialness (hey, I love foie gras, truffles and caviar just as much as the next person, but when they show up in many of the courses solely to make the course special, it takes away the point of using these ingredients!). They accept a great ingredient as special just for being itself, special!
What is challenging about Blanca's concept is that we all know that when we ourselves are preparing a meal, it's easy to create when we have our own favorite vegetables, fruits, fish and meats that are in season and at it's peak. But true creativity, sourcing and daring is when you are limited to what is available today, at it's best, and composing 27+ courses from that! That is what really impressed me about this day's menu, so kudos to everyone involved in making this meal happen. Their cooking part was the end result that we got to witness, but it was all that other stuff, sourcing, shopping, tasting, etc..., that we don't get to see, but we get to experience, that's the part of the true genius of Blanca.
Also, a special note on atmosphere and service, loved it! This was my son's 30th Birthday so we were one happy group of 12. So they let us bring in our own vinyl collection to further customize the atmosphere to our crowd. But a real big thank you to the great service provided by everyone who represented Blanca. It was refreshing to have real people explain the food who seemed genuinely as excited as me and my fellow diners and keep the whole experience totally relaxing and not so formal. The food servers who really knew their stuff, the wine pourers who keep the vino flowing, the cooks and chef for their dedication to creating something unique and special. Thank you and we'll be seeing you again soon!

I'd recommend canceling your rez and parking yourself for a tasty pizza at Roberta's instead.  I'd think about coming back if someone else made the rez and paid the bill too.  The meal is overpriced for what it is.  It's unfortunate because the first few bites started off promising with seafood accented well with "different" flavors.  After that, everything was kind of run of the mill.  Well-cooked, pretty etc but not particularly inspiring or fantastically delicious.  Filled my belly but not my memory. The eating utensils should be reviewed.  It was difficult to pick up many items with what was provided and I kept sliding my food back and forth over the plate trying to get it on my fork/spoon--something that chopsticks would solve easily.  Was nice that guests were served seconds after the first serving.  Relaxed setting and friendly staff.  Save your speed-dialing efforts for Brooklyn Fare.

--Food--
+ Wide assortment (20+ courses) of very delicate but interesting flavors.  Some courses were just amazing (i really liked the venison in daikon broth), but a few dishes were easy forgettable.

- At the time we went, Blanca did not have a liquor license, so we had to BYO.  We cannot hold this against the restaurant, but it is something to consider.

- Everyone in our party was still hungry after the meal and ended up eating again shortly after our dinner. 

--Service--
 * Casual atmosphere

 + Friendly waitstaff

 - At the $180 price point, I am forced to compare the service to similarly priced dining experiences in the city, and given this comparison, I would have to rate the service at best mediocre.  
     - There are about 20 diners per seating, and you are essentially forced to eat at the same pace as all other diners (not just your group) currently at your seating throughout the meal.
     - Also, during one of our courses one of the waitstaff forgot to plate part of the course for one of our guests -- something that would likely not happen at other similarly priced venues.


(Legend: 
   +: good
   -: bad
   *: neutral/informational)

Amazeballs. This is another top 5 meal of my life. With only 12 seats at the counter, getting a reservation here tests your patience and sanity. I spent two months trying to get in . This is by far the toughest restaurant to get in at the present moment in NYC. The cute open kitchen is tucked away in another building close to Roberta's but of course you have to walk through Roberta's first. With the tasting, you can have your choice of sparkling or still without an extra charge. As for the tasting experience, I don't remember every dish that was served but almost each one was thoughtful and creative and tasted great. Almost every single dish was executed well with everything on the dish complimenting everything else just perfectly in proportion as well as in taste, that nothing overpowered anything else. There was just perfection in every bite. The weakest part was towards the last part of the 3-hour experience, starting with the cheese plate. There was unfortunately no happy ending with the mediocre desserts that were dominated by so-so tasting sherberts and ice creams interspersed with what sounded like interesting ingredients. Each person serving you is super nice and engaging. Overall the experience was amazing. Even the leather swiveling seats at the counter were so comfortable. This is a definite must try and an invigorating breath of fresh air in the NYC dining scene. I think this place and Atera are almost on the same level with Atera beating this place handily for the innovative desserts. Both Atera and Blanca beat Brooklyn Fare any day for best new restaurants in NYC. 

Tasting:
Caviar - this delicious intro made me very hopeful for what was to come. 
Rock shrimp with celery juice and poppy seeds - so light and refreshing. I loved this one 
Platter of sashimi (included various types of white fish, sweet shrimp, and a fried shrimp head) - my favorite pieces were the sweet shrimp and the shrimp head  
Oyster - very delicious 
Beets substitute for the sweetbread - I hate sweetbread so this was good 
Wagyu sliced beef with kohl Ravi sauce - the beef was sliced very thin and each piece was just so soft, tender, and rich 
Soft tofu with apple sauce - genius combo. I have never seen apple paired with tofu like this
Pici pasta with foie gras - holy crap this was heaven. The al dente hand rolled pasta was mixed in with foie gras that has been mixed in very well as opposed to having a huge piece on top like every other restaurant that serves something similar. 
Ravioli with truffle - I could smell the truffles before the plate was set down and each bite was just so scrumptious and rich 
Chicken with polenta - this one was not my favorite since it was on the blander side compared to other dishes but apparently it is very well known 
Homemade butter with four slices of bread - good but I can't say the butter tastes any better than other butters I have tried
Alaskan king crab leg with green butter sauce - omg this was umami to the max  
Blood orange orecchiette substitute for the andouille sausage ravioli - this was also very creative and delicious 
Fried potato and sweet potato - my fave was just the sweet potato 
Grilled fish substitute for the pork - my friend said the pork was cooked perfectly but my fish was pretty good too
Steak with persimmons - wow the persimmons really complimented the sliced steak pieces. I have to note that one guy at the end of the bar got two huge pieces in addition to the bone which of course I was very jealous of. 
Melted cheese with citron sauce - I thought the citron was just so bitter and the cheese just reminded me of fondue. 
Jelly with ice cream - blah 
Caramel with ice cream - blah 
Sherbet with sun choke chips - blah
Yellow tea - this wasn't really my cup of tea as it was too bitter

Finally got a reservation to dine at Blanca after several phone calls.  On a very snowy night, we trekked our way to Bushwick and found ourselves at the non-discrete Roberta's, which was a building away from Blanca. 

Won't go into details of all the dishes we had, but some of the memorable ones include: scallops, alaskan king crab, dry aged beef, fried shrimp with head...

The good - I liked that we did not feel rushed throughout the meal and that the chefs all seemed to be very relaxed (compared to at Brooklyn Fare where all the sous-chefs seemed so tense/nervous and guests would arrive while you are halfway through the meal).

The not-so-good - The kitchen was really smokey.  Also, some of the dishes were too sour.  Some dishes were a bit too simple for what I would have expected and we also thought the sequencing of the dishes were a bit odd.  Desserts were so-so.  There were more than one "server" so it did not seem as formal (but I understand that Blanca is meant to be a "casual" restaurant.)  

The chef didn't really interact with the diners but did make quick exchanges with us during the meal.  We went during the first/second day after they obtained the liquor license - while we did not BYOD since we don't really drink, the chef kindly asked the sommelier to serve us a glass of red wine with the dry aged beef because he thought it would go well together.  We thought it was a very nice gesture.  At the end of the meal when all the guests were leaving, the chef greeted everyone farewell.
good place to eat, really liked the Soft tofu with apple sauce combo.

Came here both when it was Blanca and before when Carlo was just doing the dinners twice a week for 4 people. 

I have to say, a lot of the charm and customization is no longer there, but it was still a delicious meal. The opener course of uni and caviar - yes. Aged duck? Oh yes. But what was most impressive and memorable was actually the dessert. Blanca really steps it up there - the previous format was 27 courses and really no dessert (that I can remember...but we did drink a magnum of champagne plus 5 other bottles of wine...). 

Will I miss Carlo emailing to ask what we like to eat, and getting to respond - UNI! TRUFFLE! FOIE! GAME? Yes. Will I miss having multiple courses of uni prepared various ways? Yes. Will I miss Carlo coming by to place an entire black truffle on our table? Uhm..Duh?

But I suppose Blanca is the best of both worlds that lets more people get a taste of this experience!

For a reservation that my friend had to wake up at 5.45a PST and call 250x (not kidding. 250 times), and pay $180 pp for, I'd have to say this was good but definitely not close to the most memorable tasting menu or meal I've ever experienced. 

It's a great concept- 2 seatings a night, 12 diners per seating. The ambience is clean, contemporary and minimalistic. 
Open kitchen concept and you could see everything the chefs were doing. 

They had a very strict 'no photos' rule- so much so that when I dropped my phone and cracked the screen, and held it up to show my friends, the server hurriedly came up to me to tell me to put my phone away coz the Chef doesn't like to see cell phones. 
Ummm. 
Yea, i get that she didn't know i had just completely cracked my iPhone screen, but you'd think i was in North Korea. Puuuuleeez. 

Highlights for me were:
- Grilled Sweetbread- perfectly charred and reminded me of Japanese grill street food
- Rare beef in soup: like a classed-up pho. Very tasty
- Spicy ravioli: tasted like it was stuffed with blachan. yum
- Wagyu beef: perfectly grilled. delicious
- Sashimi plate: i enjoyed the herring tremendously. who knew?!

Everything else was not very memorable. Dessert was underwhelming.
Honestly, I'm disappointed to suggest skipping this; just go to Roberta's Pizza right next to them. You'd have a much better time and save $160

For $464 after tax and tip for two people without drinks, the cooking is expected to be flawless...and it was, however, at least every other dish is expected to be "Wow" and there the dishes failed to impress.

At a chef's table of this caliber, no dish was poorly executed.  It just wasn't scintillating to the palate; the flavors weren't strong enough in their uniqueness.  Only two dishes were amazing: the squab meat sauce pasta and the pan fried angel food cake.  Too few dishes to justify the hassle of getting a reservation and trekking to Bushwick.

I may have been spoiled by the Chef's Table at Brooklyn Fare, which impressed me on so many dishes.

2013 Michelin 1 star

Pretty much a Michelin speakeasy, located through a maze within Robertas.  They even have a bathroom speakeasy which is located behind the wall as soon as you walk in with a Japanese toilet seat.  The space is minimalistic, a counter in front of the main kitchen, seating 12.  Food was on par with 2 starred Michelin but not quite at the 3 star level.  Service was decent.  Price was about 3 starred Michelin at over $500 for party of 2 with some drinks.  The tasting runs $180, wine pairing is $92 extra.  I just ordered 2 glasses of wine, which was enough.  They also offer unpasteurized sake from japan, as well as a variety of hand crafted sodas.  The wines by the glass offering was very limited.  3 whites, 1 rose, 2 reds, and 1 orange?  Food was all pretty good, some better then others.  20+ courses of tastings.  Favorites were the 85 day dry aged wagyu beef, ravioli with andouille, agnolotti with truffle and plankton, chicken dish, and both desserts.  Staff was friendly and laid back, other patrons were kind of annoying.  *Dbag alert*  Ambiance was good with a record player playing in the background.  I would say this is on the same level as Momofuku Ko, but not quite EMP status (eleven madison park)

Enjoyed my dinner at Blanca. 20+ very small courses that mostly range from good/ very good to about a half dozen outstanding dishes. I was still hungry at course 12, and was actually toying with the idea of getting a pizza at Roberta's after dinner, but due to a wedding celebration, we exited at the street and not through Roberta's.  Most of the dishes are a bit too precious with more focus on novelty and less focus on substance. 

Favorite dishes:  agnolotti with black truffle; carrot sorbet with wheatgrass juice; pork with radishes and ice plant; wagyu beef with peaches, okra and ramps; la tour cheese with Meyer lemon purée; black olive shortbread with basil cream and strawberry; and angel food cake with tarragon cream and gooseberries. 

Service was very friendly, but sometimes difficult to hear the description of the dishes. Minimal wine list. Seats were comfortable. People were very friendly. 

No photography, cell phones, or even using a smart phone for note taking are permitted. Took notes using pen and paper. 

Bottom line: for the cost of the dinner ($180), the 7 day cancellation policy (among the most punitive in NYC), the out of the way neighborhood (Bushwick), the restriction on use of smart phones, the tiny portions, I doubt I would return.

P.S. Chef Carlo Mirarchi was not in the kitchen at Blanca during my dinner.  Perhaps if he was, I would have had a better experience.

One of the best chefs tables in NY. Took my wife who is extremely picky and the very attentive staff was happy to accommodate. The food was unreal and the drink pairing was perfect. I look forward to revisiting some time soon if we're lucky enough to get another reservation.

** 4.5 stars **

Even in a city teeming with remarkable restaurants and talent, Blanca's entry into the high-end tasting menu scene commanded attention.  Located in a gentrifying but still gritty, working class neighborhood in Brooklyn, a borough rarely recognized for its culinary work nationally or internationally.  It is the latest development in the organic growth of its chef's work, a side project at Roberta's.

Limited to six seatings a week, 12 diners at a time at a counter, an increasingly popular model less egalitarian than tables; cost notwithstanding, it can be near impossible to secure a seat.  The process has recently transitioned from phone to online, seats opening 30 days prior to dining date.

Blanca has no direct public entrance.  Guests check-in at Roberta's front desk, and are escorted separately to Blanca via a labyrinthine path; like a secret passageway, the background noise of Roberta's crowds heightening the contrast.

The first impression upon entering Blanca is of unexpected spaciousness.  One senses it was not designed as a restaurant.  The set-up is essentially a professional grade kitchen that happens to have a counter planted on one side for diners, like voyeurs, to watch the show.  Apropos at a time when watching a kitchen in action is routine, televised entertainment.  Work stations are arranged to facilitate viewing of each step of food preparation and plating for successive courses.  There isn't a bad seat in the house.

The stark white and gleaming silver surfaces of the kitchen feel aseptic, but that is as it should be.  Although the space itself could never be called warm, diners need not want for comfort.  The upholstered, swivel bar chairs are sturdy and plush.  There's a turntable with LPs that guests may play.  Freshen up in a roomy bathroom with a Japanese toilet, behind a curtain framed by an Asian-style wood lattice.  Belongings go on shelves behind the seats, including cell phones and cameras.  Blanca's current policies do not permit photography, although note-taking gets a pass.

The staff do much to elevate the experience.  As attentive, polished, and proficient as a fine white-cloth dining venue, but with a rare, easy friendliness that is disarming and refreshing.  The dining counter actually facilitates a degree of intimacy with the staff impossible with a traditional table set-up, which made their poise and confidence all the more important.  They met that challenge, treating guests warmly, knowledgeably describing courses, and ensuring the parade of plates hummed along smoothly.  

With chef Carlo Mirarchi working but keeping a low profile, the kitchen started shortly after reservation time.  He served some of the courses himself, but without fanfare.  Based on online descriptions, the number and types of courses remain consistent, with frequent seasonal variation.  

The courses, near as I recollect sans note-taking, were:
     Basque cider
     Osetra caviar w/parsnip cream
     Cherry in almond milk
     Fried sweetbread w/kaffir lime
     Potato and sweet potato w/buttermilk, chrysanthemum leaf, & watercress juice
     Aged pork
     Wagyu beef in kohlrabi broth
     Tofu w/pea puree
     Sea perch
     Crudo (octopus, sardine, glass shrimp, bonito, cobia, herring)
     Agnolotti w/shaved black truffle & plankton
     Pici pasta w/shaved geoduck
     Nduja ravioli w/Calabrian chile
     Carrot sorbet 
     Bread course (whole wheat, baguette, buckwheat walnut, semi white)
     Pork loin
     King crab w/plankton butter sauce
     Dry aged steak
     Roast Sasso chicken
     Cucumber sorbet w/gin granita
     La Tur cheese on citron
     Strawberry dessert w/meringue
     Toasted angel food shortcake
     Mint tea
     Mezcal macaron, ginger candy

The quality of the food and preparation was almost universally exceptional.  The impact of some ingredient pairings were startling, such as a dab of parsnip cream on salty caviar, or subtly sweet kohlrabi with rich, silky Wagyu slices or smooth housemade tofu with fresh, sweet pea puree.  Wonderful baked breads with salt butter needed no further accompaniment.  Delicious crudo, each paired with a complementary flavor or ingredient.  Best of all were from the pasta courses: the agnolotti, each one an utterly perfect earthy mouthful of flavor, and the luscious, spicy Nduja ravioli.  Among the most memorable bites of late.  The only low was from over-salted chicken.  There was more than enough food by meal's end.

An upscale dining experience, with a pleasing, scruffy Brooklyn touch.  A very fine tasting menu that ranks among the best I've had, with many unique and memorable creations.  As a whole, not as cohesive and seamless as I've had elsewhere but that rough edge is part of its excitement.  Blanca deserves its reputation, and is worth the effort to go.  Currently $180 per person, an additional $85 for a pairing that may include beer, wine, and sake.

I had dinner at Blanca last week.  I was seated next to a food critic.  While the food critic and I both sat at the same bar, had the same menu, ordered the same wine pairing, the experience couldn't be more different.  

The food critic's wine was constantly topped off while mine was left empty.  His steak was still attached to the bone while mine was two little pieces.  I was told I couldn't check my email on my phone while the food critic was constantly on his email with no objections from the staff.

The double standards left the experience very wanting.
A nice meal but in my opinion nothing special.  We liked every course but did not find any of them to be particularly memorable.   Overall not worth the cost and effort to schlep to the slums

Am actually goin against Public  Enemy  on this one. DO believe the Hype! This place is all that and a bag of chips. One of the most interesting, enjoyable meals I've had in the U.S. A lot of the props rests squarely on the shoulders of Leslie, Shanti and Toto ;-)))
Run, don't walk my friends. You never know how long a star like this will burn bright
(Sometimes they leave us quickly when they are burning at they're brightest  i.e.  Ubuntu....)

Blanca!  Fantastic.  23 unique, interesting, and above all.. delicious courses!  The best word to describe the evening is "experience".  A great experience it was.  Great food, great service, and even great music (they have a turntable and a diverse collection of vinyl that the guests can choose from).
Special props go to Rose and the chefs for making special accommodations and food substitutions for my fiancé, who does not eat red meat.   They even gave us an anniversary card at the end of the night.  Thoughtful presentation.
And a special shout-out goes to our seatmate Carol C (the previous reviewer), and her guests.  A fun night had by all.

Overall I think it was a "good" experience, but a ton to be desired.

1. Fish - Excellent
2. Meat - Excellent
3. Pasta - embarrassing. Under cooked and absolutely no balance to sauces. 
4. Spices and vegetables - Excellent
5. Plating - Excellent
6. Wine pairing - horrible

OK, so it is a solid place and a cool vibe of course, but for the $195 price tag which is up there with the 3 michelin star restaurants around the city, you might not leave satisfied.  No joke, my buddy and I went and had the meal and then got a table in Roberta's and killed a pizza!  And the pizza was one of the best things we had for the night.  Portions are tiny, as with most tasting menus, but you really don't get anything close to an entree.  A few dishes were definitely oversalted- and if you are looking for modern techniques with plays on texture, you won't find that here.  Fresh ingredients, good flavors, sure - but based on the menu I had and the location in industrial Bushwick there is no way the food cost/overhead warrants the price of the menu - there were virtually no "luxurious" ingredients that you would expect.  Also, you are in Brooklyn, offer some reasonable wines by the glass instead of clearly trying to rope people in to the wine/beer/sake pairing.  The only two reds by the glass are $36 and $38 per glass.  We got a bottle of cherry beer that was $42!  Plus, there will most likely be confusion in your seating- we registered at Roberta's and then waiting at the bar area and nobody got us.  In turn, we came close to missing the first course, but we did get the last seats on the end of the bar.  BTW, reservations are much easier now on their web site.  A few memorable and amazing dishes did come out of this meal, the nduja ravioli stands out, the single slice of dry aged steak, the little corn and tomato dish was fresh and tasty.  Dessert course was underwhelming as was the crudo.  Was the pastry chef absent the day we were there?  A small cheese course that was good but again lacked any contrast in texture, and a fresh wheat grass ice cream was a nice palette cleanser but Jean Georges or any of the other big boys would blow you away with their dessert while I was left asking for more......

I celebrated my friend's birthday at Blanca last week.

While the food was innovative and unique, I couldn't help to think that only a few (out of many) that were mind blowing. If that. Maybe our expectations were too high, maybe we went on an off night. Maybe I'm just not a fan of ultra esoteric cuisine, or one bite dishes. (for example grapefruit cavatelli) But I was fortunate enough to have dinner at El Bulli in the past and that was strange but the steak tartare with frozen uni crumble WORKED there.

You know that feeling when you keep wishing and praying that it gets better, you start trying to convince yourself that what you're having is genius, or beyond anything you've ever experienced. Almost like that Acadamey Award winning movie that everyone talks about, but you just don't "get?" Then I looked over to the people to the left and right of us and they weren't that wowed either. Sure, there were some great things, but for a middle class earning foodie, I kept wishing we just went to one of the Momofuku restaurants and called it a day.

For the hassle of schlepping to some off the beaten path speak easy type restaurant to the drama of getting a reservation, I just don't think its worth it.

For dinner for two with a few glasses of wine here and there, the $600 price tag wasn't as appetizing as other remarkable "special" dinners we've had in the past (Eleven Madison, Le Bernadin, Per Se) 

I would rather have dropped a few extra hundred dollars and repeated the remarkable dinners we've had at Per Se. But we didn't feel like making a production and their casual dress code + "fancy" food policy we just couldn't resist.

If you have a shitload of money to blow and the time to get a reservation, maybe this place is for you. I was reminded of the time we went to Aquavit for a tasting (that was better than this) and left hungry- we stopped off at Wendy's for burgers on the way home. Fortunately, we were able to make it to Pies and Thighs for some incredible doughnuts to top off the night!

I apologize in advance if this review pisses anybody off, I swear I'm not a naysayer. I'm just keeping it real.

Oh Blanca! Crossed the Williamsburg bridge to dine with you! Im so sorry to tell you, after tasting 25 courses that there is not a single one I can remember. Awesome space, the food fell short. I wish I had saved the $650.00 and just grabbed a beer and a pie at Roberta's.  Keep the friendly cool staff.....and find a way to bold up the meal. I walked out of those doors feeling robbed. Robbed for my time and my money.

Rating 3.5

Blanca isn't as hard to get reservations for as other chef's tables.  Dinner was solid and blanca really shines in the meat entrees.  Their homemade pancetta was out of this world.  The crudo course was great with different raw fishes that I've never tried before.  There were other dishes that weren't as memorable and that cilantro ice cream at the end is not for everyone!  Overall, it's a good place to try a chef's table if you're just starting out experiencing innovative food.  Unfortunately I went from Brooklyn Fare to here and it doesn't quite meet that standard.

A unique experience that I won't soon forget.  Regarding the food, as you may know, there are more than twenty courses.  Some of the courses are excellent, others are good and some I didn't like. 

The coolest part is actually being served all those dishes with a small number of people in comfortable chairs facing an open kitchen. The service was actually quite good and we felt comfortable.  Dinner is nearly three hours but went by somewhat quickly.  Considering the many courses, it always felt like something was going on.

So why only three stars?  The food overall was good but nothing amazing.  And for the type of money we spent, I expected exceptional. I'm glad we dined at Blanca but doubt we'll be back.

Crazy lucky--noticed a Zagat posting that just ranked Blanca as #1 restaurant in NYC--saw that it has a Michelin star--and (amazingly!!) got reservations for 2 that opened up at Blanca on day of--and WOW--what an incredible once-in-a-lifetime meal!  Do not miss this one!  So so fun with the 'wine pairing' (which is actually a champagne, wine, port, beer, sake pairing--so perfect). I am thinking that Blanca is not yet discovered by the broader foodie audience...but once it is...it will not be so easy to get those reservations--so check it out soon!!

Our dearest friends took us here for the most amazing dinner ! From the moment I have walked in, I felt like Alice in Wonderland - the restaurant is hidden behind a pizza parlor, so to enter it's warm cozy environment, one must go through rather an elaborate path and gracefully skirt over tons of Williamsburg hipsters vicariously porking out on pizza. 

Old warehouses and bleak buildings nearby only help create sensation of the miracle once you walk in and see for yourself the contrast between gleamy outside and glamorous inside. You begin to think to yourself: wow, it was totally worth it to come here all the way from the city! 

Ahhhhh, the dinner !  What can be said about the dinner ? It was well portioned and perfectly served. The food was great, I would have appreciated more vegetable courses however. The meat lovers seemed pleased by many red meat courses. The wine pairings were a bit off, especially the reds left us to desire more. However, the customer service shined and the night was perfect ! It helped that we were amongst a great company, but overall Shanti ( the restaurant manager as I understood) was a shining star and made us feel welcome, warm and happy to be dining there on that night ! 

I can not wait to come back and see what tasty treats they have in store for us next time!

This is one of my all time favorite dining experiences.  The numerous courses were absolutely delicious and the ambiance is a great, chill experience -- playing interesting vinyls that makes you enjoy the food without a pretentious reverence. 

Too many dishes to list. It wouldn't be fair to give you any recos. The tasting menu spans a range of cuisines... Italian, Japanese, and some worldly bites that can't be categorized. 

Greet place for a special occasion. 

(We went 2 months ago, and just finished this review that was sitting in my drafts)

Go.

You know you're in for something special when one of the most intoxicating broths you've ever had was coaxed out of a rutabaga.

Really? Rutabaga?

Not just rutabaga, but kohlrabi as well.  I was taken aback not just by the consistency and balance of bold and captivating flavours and profiles, but by the intensity they were able to coax out of just a few elements.  The intensity of a single morsel of garlic scape that cut through the soft tofu and sweet apple broth; the unexpected brightness and balance that a tiny rind of kumquat could bring to a deeply satisfying cut of duck breast; and the progression of perfection through a course of octopus, sardines, sea perch, and mackerel that elevated you higher and higher with each bite - all so simple, but all so infinitely sublime.

I loved that every course of beef was a perfectly treated cut of Wagyu, and the use of a marvelously tender pork collar was a refreshing change from the usual belly.  My eyebrows were raised when served a plankton agnolotti (weird but tasty!), but my tastebuds stood at attention with the blast of heat and spice of the 'Nduja sausage ravioli (get it all in one bite!).  

The sweets were equally delightful: I've never had a spicy but refreshing pepper cress sorbet with wheat grass juice before, but it perfectly transitioned us between two luxurious beef and duck courses.  I also can't stop thinking about the cold-smoked ricotta cheese gelato, paired beautifully with a pine nut gelato and Persian limes.

All in all, an outstanding meal.  I still can't get over not only how many dishes they were able to crank out, but how each one was just so perfectly and consistently executed and brilliantly thought out.  Without the (overt) bells and whistles of molecular gastronomy, I would comfortably compare the level of creativeness and development of ingredients approaching that which I experienced at Alinea, while clearly maintaining the clear goal of ultimately cooking delicious tasting food throughout.  

This is definitely a meal to treat yourself and a loved one to at some point in your life, and one that you will both most definitely relish.  And if anyone is wondering: yes, it's totally fine to wear jeans.
